source_text: וּ֥/תְהִי ע֨וֹד נֶ֘חָ֤מָתִ֗/י וַ/אֲסַלְּדָ֣ה בְ֭/חִילָה לֹ֣א יַחְמ֑וֹל כִּי לֹ֥א כִ֝חַ֗דְתִּי אִמְרֵ֥י קָדֽוֹשׁ׀־׃
english_snapshot: This would still be my comfort, and I would exult in unrelenting pain[a]; for I have not denied the words of the Holy One.

signals.text: The Hebrew of this clause is difficult and compressed. More literally, it may be read, “and I would exult in pain; he does not spare.” The rare verb rendered “exult” may instead describe a forceful movement.

source_text: כִּֽי עַ֭תָּה הֱיִ֣יתֶם לא תִּֽרְא֥וּ חֲ֝תַ֗ת וַ/תִּירָֽאוּ־׃
english_snapshot: For now you have become nothing[a]; you see terror[b], and you are afraid.

signals.text: Hebrew literally reads something like 'you have become not.' Many understand the sense as 'you have become nothing' or 'you have become like it,' that is, like the unreliable streams in the preceding verses.

source_text: אַֽ֭דַבְּרָה וְ/לֹ֣א אִירָאֶ֑/נּוּ כִּ֥י לֹא כֵ֥ן אָ֝נֹכִ֗י עִמָּדִֽ/י־׃
english_snapshot: Then I would speak and not fear him, for it is not so with me.[a]

signals.text: The Hebrew final clause is elliptical; more literally, “for not so am I with myself.”

source_text: הֵ֣ן יִ֭קְטְלֵ/נִי לא אֲיַחֵ֑ל אַךְ דְּ֝רָכַ֗/י אֶל פָּנָ֥י/ו אוֹכִֽיחַ־־׃
english_snapshot: Though he slay me, I will not wait; yet I will argue my ways before him.[a]

signals.text: A traditional alternative reading is “Though he slay me, yet I will hope in him.” It reads לוֹ, “in him,” rather than the WLC’s לֹא, “not.”

source_text: לְ֭/חֵלֶק יַגִּ֣יד רֵעִ֑ים וְ/עֵינֵ֖י בָנָ֣י/ו תִּכְלֶֽנָה׃
english_snapshot: One who denounces friends for a share[a]—his children’s eyes will fail.

signals.text: The first clause is difficult. “A share” may mean a portion or gain, and the verb translated “denounces” more literally means “declares” or “reports.”

source_text: אָבִ֗י יִבָּחֵ֣ן אִיּ֣וֹב עַד נֶ֑צַח עַל תְּ֝שֻׁבֹ֗ת בְּ/אַנְשֵׁי אָֽוֶן־־־׃
english_snapshot: Oh[a], let Job be tested to the limit[b] because of his answers like those of wicked men[c].

signals.text: The Masoretic Hebrew is vocalized “my father,” but in this difficult line the expression is commonly understood as introducing a wish: “Oh” or “Would that.”
